newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Travel, tourism seen as major source of new jobs.
newsitem.headline: Travel, tourism seen as major source of new jobs.

text.p: The travel and tourism industry should create 135 million new jobs worldwide over the next decade, a senior industry official said on Tuesday.

"Our industry generates 250 million jobs today across the global economy, representing just over 10 percent of the workforce," Geoffrey Lipman, president of the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC), told a news conference.
"Over the next 10 years we can jump up that number to 385 million," he said, referring to jobs in travel, tourism and dependent sectors such as construction and retailing.
The WTTC represents more than 80 chief executive officers from all sectors of the global travel and tourism industry.
Its goal is to work with governments to promote job creation in the industry, open and competitive markets, development and elimination of barriers to growth.
Lipman said improving living standards, services-driven economies and more open societies would boost demand sharply for travel and tourism into the 21st century, notably in Asia.
"We expect to see twice as many travellers over the next 10 years. Many Chinese will start travelling. There will be more women and young travellers," he said.

Lipman and other senior international tourism officials were visiting Lisbon to promote a travel and tourism world summit to be held in Vilamoura in the Algarve in southern Portugal between January 17-19 next year.
The conference will bring together policymakers and senior private sector officials to discuss the future of the travel and tourism industry and its potential to create jobs.

"The most important question at the conference will be: 'Why should policymakers care about travel and tourism, and what steps should be taken to develop the industry?'" said Harvey Golub, chairman and chief executive officer of American Express Co, who is also chairman of the WTTC.
Lipman said: "There is no government in the world that does not see employment as a top priority issue.
"We want governments to see travel and tourism as a strategic industry and to help us eliminate barriers to growth," he added, flanked by Portuguese Economy Minister Augusto Mateus.

Lipman said hurdles to industrial development included inadequate infrastructure in many countries, such as roads, railways and airports; over-taxation; and the need of the workforce to adapt to the growing number of travellers.
"We know we have to pay our taxes, but we object to the add-on taxes -- the special taxes on travel, such as hotel and airport taxes," he said.
"We have to develop good careers in tourism to provide the right sort of training to meet the linguistic and cultural needs of travellers," he added.
